summary: Without a way to carry the encoding type of an ISDN subaddress, interworking between ISUP networks and SIP networks is impossible in some cases. This informational document specifies a new optional tel URI parameter to carry that encoding type.

plainLanguage.summary: Old phone networks sometimes add a tiny extra address to a number. This adds a label to the phone-number link saying how that extra address is written.

questions: how do gateways translate isdn subaddresses
subtitle: Specify encoding for subaddresses in telephone URIs.

tldr.problem: When translating between ISDN and SIP networks, subaddress encoding information is lost. Gateways cannot know how to translate the subaddress correctly without this information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4715 adds an optional "isub-encoding" parameter to tel URIs that carries the encoding type (IA5, BCD, or other) used for ISDN subaddresses.
tldr.outcome: SIP and ISDN networks can now reliably exchange subaddress information without losing or misinterpreting the encoding type.

today: RFC 4715 is an Informational RFC published in November 2006 and has not been obsoleted. It provides an optional extension to RFC 3966 for improved ISDN and SIP interoperability.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3966 defines a tel URI parameter called isub to carry Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) subaddresses. These subaddresses are extra routing information added to phone numbers in traditional telephone networks.

However, RFC 3966 does not specify how to indicate the encoding type of the subaddress. In ISDN systems, subaddresses can be encoded different ways: International Alphabet 5 (IA5), Binary Coded Decimal (BCD), or other formats defined in ISO 8348. Without knowing which encoding was used, gateways translating between ISDN and Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) networks cannot properly reconstruct the original subaddress.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone subaddress is like an apartment number added to a street address. The problem is that the same digits can be written in different ways, and you need to know which way was used.

sections.title: The Interworking Problem
sections.content:
Two scenarios create problems. First, when a SIP device sends a call with an isub parameter to an ISDN terminal, the gateway cannot know which encoding to use when translating the SIP message into an ISUP (ISDN User Part) message. It might choose the wrong encoding, creating an incorrect subaddress at the ISDN terminal.

Second, when routing between two ISDN networks through a SIP network (ISDN-SIP-ISDN), the encoding type information in the original ISUP message is lost when translated to SIP. When the second gateway tries to translate back to ISUP, it cannot reconstruct the correct subaddress because the encoding type is missing.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a postcard that says "12345" addressed to apartment 12345. But if the apartment number is actually using a special number code, you need to decode it first. If the gateway doesn't know which code was used, it delivers the wrong number.

sections.title: The isub-encoding Parameter
sections.content:
RFC 4715 introduces an optional isub-encoding parameter for tel URIs. This parameter tells gateways and SIP entities which encoding format was used for the subaddress value in the isub parameter.

Three encoding values are defined. nsap-ia5 indicates the subaddress uses IA5 encoding (AFI=0x50), the most common type. nsap-bcd indicates Binary Coded Decimal encoding (AFI=0x48). nsap indicates other NSAP address encodings defined in ISO 8348, with the encoding type embedded in the first two characters of the isub value as hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameter is like adding a note saying "the apartment number is written in code A" or "code B" or "some other code". Now receivers know exactly how to read it.

sections.title: Gateway and SIP Entity Behavior
sections.content:
When a gateway receives an ISDN message with a subaddress, it checks the encoding type and sets the isub-encoding parameter accordingly. If the subaddress was IA5, the gateway may omit the parameter (defaulting to IA5) or set it to nsap-ia5. For BCD encoding, it must set isub-encoding to nsap-bcd and decode the subaddress into decimal digits. For other encodings, it sets isub-encoding to nsap and encodes the entire NSAP address as hexadecimal in the isub parameter.

A compliant SIP entity follows the reverse logic. If isub-encoding is absent, it assumes IA5 encoding. If the parameter is present, it encodes the isub value appropriately for the ISUP message it is creating. Non-compliant entities simply ignore the parameter and treat the message as if it were absent.
sections.plainLanguage: When translating between phone systems, the gateway looks at the encoding label and translates the number correctly. If there's no label, it assumes the most common type. Old systems just ignore the label and do their best.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The isub-encoding parameter should be used whenever the encoding of the ISDN subaddress is not IA5. When isub-encoding is absent and an isub parameter is present, RFC 4715 requires that the original encoding be assumed to be IA5 (AFI=0x50). This ensures backward compatibility with existing systems that do not yet support the new parameter.

The RFC explicitly notes that "user specified" subaddress types are beyond its scope. Additionally, no new security considerations arise from this parameter; it inherits the security model from RFC 3966.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is optional, but gateways that understand it can translate more accurately. Systems that don't know about the label still work by assuming the most common type.
